content: The International AIDS Society published a study in 2019 (Volume 22, Supplement 1, Article e25255) that analyzed the costs associated with distributing differentiated HIV self-testing kits in Zambia. Ahmed and colleagues presented this research at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) held in Boston, USA, in March 2018, with findings summarized in Top Antiviral Medicine (page 454s). Medley et al. evaluated the outcomes and costs of three strategies aimed at increasing HIV testing among male partners in South Africa. This study was presented at the 2019 CROI in Seattle, USA. Huang and colleagues assessed the cost-effectiveness of promoting HIV self-testing through Grindr™, a smartphone-based social networking application. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2015 (Volume 91, Supplement 2, pages A226-A). Cambiano et al. conducted an assessment of the potential impact and cost-effectiveness of HIV self-testing in low-income countries. Their findings were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2015 (Volume 212, Issue 4, pages 570-577). Another study by Cambiano and colleagues, published in Topics in Antiviral Medicine in 2017, explored the cost-effectiveness of various delivery approaches for HIV self-testing, presented at the 24th CROI. Further, Cambiano et al. analyzed the impact and cost-effectiveness of community-based HIV self-testing in sub-Saharan Africa through a health economic and modeling approach. This research was published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2019. Maheswaran and colleagues examined the cost-effectiveness of community-based HIV self-testing in Blantyre, Malawi, with findings published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2018 (Volume 66, Issue 8, pages 1211-1221). Indravudh et al. developed a protocol for a cluster-randomized trial to evaluate community-led delivery of HIV self-testing in rural Malawi. This study aimed to improve HIV testing, antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, and broader social outcomes. The protocol was published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2019 (Volume 19, Article 814). Yang et al. highlighted the importance of people-centered social innovation in HIV services for key populations in Asia. This work is currently in press. The World Health Organization (WHO) released consolidated guidelines on self-care interventions for sexual and reproductive health and rights, accessible online as of September 3, 2019. Additionally, WHO provided guidance on couples' HIV testing and counseling, including recommendations for antiretroviral therapy for serodiscordant couples, published in 2012. Semple et al. studied the uptake of a partner notification model for HIV among men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender women in Tijuana, Mexico. Their findings were published in AIDS and Behavior in 2018 (Volume 22, Issue 7, pages 2042-2055). Little et al. shared insights from implementing an HIV-assisted partner notification intervention in Central Asia, published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2019 (Volume 22, Supplement 3, Article e25313). Carballo-Diéguez et al. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2002 (Volume 29, Issue 8, pages 465-471). Baytop et al. compared strategies to increase HIV testing among African-American gay, bisexual, and other MSM in Washington, DC. Their findings were published in AIDS Care in 2014 (Volume 26, Issue 5, pages 608-612). Cabrera Oliva et al. investigated whether online interventions could enhance HIV case finding and linkage to care among MSM and transgender women in Central America. This study was presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2018. Clark et al. compared sampling methodologies for epidemiologic surveillance of MSM and transgender women in Latin America. Their findings were published in AIDS and Behavior in 2014 (Volume 18, Issue 12, pages 2338-2348). Ellen et al. evaluated recruitment approaches to identify newly diagnosed HIV infections among African-American MSM. This study was published in the International Journal of STD & AIDS in 2013 (Volume 24, Issue 5, pages 335-339). Flavien et al. implemented an incentivized community-driven intervention to promote HIV testing among clients of sex workers. This study was presented at the International AIDS Society Conference in Paris in 2017. Guo et al. compared four sampling methods among MSM in China, with implications for HIV/STD surveillance and prevention. Their findings were published in AIDS Care in 2011 (Volume 23, Issue 11, pages 1400-1409). Halkitis et al. evaluated the effectiveness of three HIV testing strategies targeting African-American MSM in New York City. This study was published in Annals of Behavioral Medicine in 2011 (Volume 42, Issue 3, pages 361-369). Ifekandu et al. explored the use of social networking to reach hard-to-reach MSM subpopulations in Lagos, Nigeria. This study was presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2018. Kan et al. utilized social network methods for HIV case-finding among people who inject drugs in Tajikistan. Their findings were published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2018 (Volume 21, Supplement 5, Article e25139). Katz et al. demonstrated that partner services for sexually transmitted diseases increased HIV testing among partners of MSM. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2016 (Volume 43, Supplement, pages S207-S). Lightfoot et al. used a social network strategy to distribute HIV self-test kits to African-American and Latino MSM. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2018 (Volume 79, Issue 1, pages 38-45). Lillie et al. implemented performance-based incentives and social networks to increase HIV case-finding among key populations in Côte d’Ivoire. This study was presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2018. Potasin et al. enhanced HIV testing coverage through peer-driven recruitment models among transgender women in Pattaya. This study was presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2018. Smyrnov et al. applied a risk network approach to locate undiagnosed HIV cases in Odessa, Ukraine. Their findings were published in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2018 (Volume 21, Issue 1). Carballo-Diéguez et al. This study was published in AIDS and Behavior in 2012 (Volume 16, Issue 7, pages 1753-1760). Linjongrat et al. discussed increasing domestic financing for civil society organizations in the HIV response through accreditation of HIV clinical services provided by key populations. This study was presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2018. Thirumurthy et al. promoted male partner HIV testing and safer sexual decision-making through secondary distribution of self-tests by HIV-negative female sex workers and women receiving antenatal and postpartum care in Kenya. This cohort study was published in The Lancet HIV in 2016 (Volume 3, Issue 6, pages e266-274). Beougher et al. examined motivations to test for HIV among partners in concordant HIV-negative and HIV-discordant gay male couples. This study was published in Archives of Sexual Behavior in 2015 (Volume 44, Issue 2, pages 499-508). Carballo-Diéguez et al. investigated whether gay and bisexual men at high risk of infection would use over-the-counter rapid HIV tests to screen sexual partners. This study was published in the Journal of Sex Research in 2012 (Volume 49, Issue 4, pages 379-387). Chanda et al. identified barriers and facilitators to HIV testing among Zambian female sex workers in three transit hubs. This study was published in AIDS Patient Care and STDs in 2017 (Volume 31, Issue 7, pages 290-296). Fields et al. explored the use of geosocial networking apps to access young Black gay, bisexual, and other MSM at risk for HIV. This study was published in the American Journal of Health Promotion in 2019. Godbole et al. improved access to HIV testing among hard-to-reach sex workers in India by providing testing services at their doorstep. This study was presented at the 9th IAS Conference on HIV Science in Paris, France, in 2017. Maman et al. conducted a qualitative study on the secondary distribution of HIV self-test kits by female sex workers in Kenya. This study was published in PLOS One in 2017 (Volume 12, Issue 3, Article e0174629). Mitchell and Sullivan examined relationship and demographic factors associated with the willingness to use an in-home rapid HIV test to screen potential sexual partners among HIV-negative and HIV-discordant male couples in the US. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2015 (Volume 69, Issue 2, pages 252-256). Sharma et al. assessed the willingness of MSM in the US to distribute free rapid home HIV test kits and test with social or sexual network associates. This study was published in AIDS Care in 2017 (Volume 29, Issue 12, pages 1499-1503). Tobin et al. evaluated the acceptability and feasibility of a peer mentor program to train young Black MSM to promote HIV and STI home-testing to their social network members. This study was published in AIDS Care in 2018 (Volume 30, Issue 7, pages 896-902). Woodward et al. conducted a computer-assisted survey of attitudes toward HIV and STI partner notification among HIV-positive MSM. This study was published in Sexual Health in 2010 (Volume 7, Issue 4, pages 460-462). Xu et al. examined the acceptability and feasibility of promoting HIV testing to sexual partners using self-testing among HIV-positive MSM in Guangzhou, China. This study was presented at the 22nd International AIDS Conference in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2018. Golden et al. demonstrated the effectiveness of peer referral for HIV case-finding among MSM. This study was published in AIDS in 2006 (Volume 20, Issue 15, pages 1961-1968). Solomon et al. utilized respondent-driven sampling to identify HIVand HCV-infected people who inject drugs and MSM in India. This study was published in PLOS Medicine in 2017 (Volume 14, Issue 11, Article e1002460). Zulliger et al. evaluated the cost-utility of HIV testing programs among MSM in the US. This study was published in AIDS and Behavior in 2017 (Volume 21, Issue 3, pages 619-625).
